abstract.p: Osmotic stress represents a major challenge to cells, particularly in the kidney, where tonicity gradients are both physiologically relevant and pathologically altered. The transcription factor nuclear factor of activated T cells 5 (NFAT5) is a key regulator of the osmoadaptive response, yet its downstream metabolic effectors remain incompletely understood. In this study, we identify the glycolytic side-branch enzyme 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate mutase (BPGM) as a transcriptional NFAT5 target that is induced under hypertonic conditions. RNA-seq analysis revealed that Bpgm knockdown significantly alters gene expression under osmotic stress (450 mOsmol/kg), with substantial overlap between BPGM- and NFAT5-responsive transcriptional programs. Bpgm depletion impairs the induction of canonical NFAT5 target genes, suggesting a functional interplay between metabolic and transcriptional adaptation. Promoter enrichment analysis showed that genes regulated by both NFAT5 and BPGM under hypertonic conditions are associated with CpG islands and GC-rich elements, supporting a link to chromatin structure and transcriptional accessibility. Consistently, we show that HIF-1α expression is regulated downstream of NFAT5 and BPGM, indicating a hierarchical organization of osmotic and hypoxic stress responses. We propose that BPGM facilitates NFAT5 function through metabolic-epigenetic coupling, acting as an amplifier of protective gene expression. Notably, this axis is active in BPGM-expressing cells such as those of the distal convoluted tubule. Thus, our findings establish BPGM as a critical node in the osmoadaptive gene regulatory network and highlight how cell type-specific metabolic profiles influence the transcriptional response to hypertonic stress.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Osmotic stress is a fundamental physiological challenge encountered by cells and tissues in various organ systems. The equilibrium osmolarity of the body is one of the most tightly controlled physiological parameter [1]. In normal physiological conditions, sodium plays a key role in regulating osmotic shifts between body water compartments, as it predominantly determines extracellular osmolality [2]. It arises when the extracellular osmolarity deviates from homeostatic conditions, prompting adaptive responses to maintain cellular function and integrity [3]. In clinical contexts, osmotic stress is particularly relevant in conditions such as dehydration, hyperglycemia, and kidney disease, where fluctuations in osmotic balance can lead to severe cellular dysfunction and organ damage [4]. The kidney, as the primary regulator of water and electrolyte homeostasis, is especially susceptible to osmotic stress due to its function in concentrating urine and maintaining systemic osmolarity. Within the kidney, different nephron segments experience varying degrees of osmotic stress, with the renal medulla being exposed to extreme hyperosmotic conditions [5]. This requires precise regulatory mechanisms to ensure cellular survival and function under these challenging conditions.

A critical player in the cellular response to osmotic stress is the transcription factor nuclear factor of activated T cells 5 (NFAT5), also known as tonicity-responsive enhancer-binding protein (TonEBP) [6]. NFAT5 is unique among the NFAT family members as it is specifically activated in response to hypertonic stress rather than calcium-dependent signaling pathways [7]. The primary role of NFAT5 is to orchestrate the transcription of genes involved in osmoprotective mechanisms, including osmolyte transporters, heat shock proteins, and metabolic regulators, thereby enabling cells to withstand hyperosmotic conditions [8]. In the kidney, NFAT5 plays a pivotal role in the adaptation of tubular epithelial cells to osmotic fluctuations, especially in the renal medulla, where high interstitial osmolarity demands robust cellular defenses, e.g., against hypovolemic stress or in diabetes mellitus. Dysregulation of NFAT5 activity has been implicated in various renal pathologies, including acute kidney injury (AKI) [9] and chronic kidney disease (CKD) [10], where impaired osmoadaptation can exacerbate inflammation, fibrosis, and cell death [11–13].

We recently demonstrated that 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate mutase (BPGM), expressed in kidney tubular cells, plays a protective role against reactive oxygen species (ROS) and apoptosis under hyperosmotic stress conditions [14]. Traditionally, BPGM has been associated with erythrocytes, where it regulates the oxygen affinity to hemoglobin by producing 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG), a key glycolytic intermediate [15]. For decades, its function was thought to be limited to red blood cells. However, recent findings indicate a broader physiological relevance, with BPGM expression detected in the placenta [16], astrocytes [17], cancer cells [18], myocardial tissue [19] and the kidney [14]. Constitutive renal BPGM expression in the distal nephron plays a crucial role in renal homeostasis by modulating glucose metabolism. This challenges the conventional understanding of BPGM and highlights its potential significance in non-erythroid tissues.

Despite the well-established role of NFAT5 in orchestrating osmoprotective transcriptional programs in the kidney [20–22], the characterization and functional relevance of its downstream metabolic effectors remain incompletely understood. Recent studies have shown that BPGM is renoprotective and strongly induced under hypertonic conditions [14], but its integration into NFAT5-dependent osmoadaptive signaling and its role beyond canonical glycolytic function have not yet been systematically investigated. In particular, it is unknown whether BPGM is under direct transcriptional control of NFAT5 and whether BPGM-dependent metabolic alterations contribute to the regulation of NFAT5 target genes. This represents a relevant conceptual gap in our understanding of how osmoadaptive transcriptional responses interface with cellular metabolism.

Here, we address whether BPGM acts as a metabolic effector downstream of NFAT5 and explore its role in coupling metabolic state to adaptive transcriptional responses during hypertonic stress in renal tubular cells.

sec.title: Animals
sec.p: For animal experiments KspCre-deleter mice were used to generate congenital tubular knockouts of either Bpgm (Bpgm-KO) or Nfat5 (Nfat5-KO) in the kidney. Specifically, mice carrying the floxed Bpgm allele (Bpgmtm1a(KOMP)Wtsi (ESC clone ID; EPD0190_5_G03, Sanger Institute) were bred to mice expressing Cre recombinase under the control of the murine kidney-specific cadherin-16 promoter (ksp-cre+), resulting in recombinase activity in the distal nephron segments [23]. Age-matched C57BL/6 N wild-type mice (Jackson Laboratory) served as controls. Animals between 5 and 21 weeks of age were included in the study. Knockout was verified using qPCR (Supplementary Figure S1). The generation of Nfat5-KO mice (Aqp2Cre+/−Nfat5fl/fl and KspCre+/−Nfat5fl/fl) [24] and their respective controls with verification was previously described in Engel K & Kulow VA et al. [13]. Briefly, to generate Nfat5-deficient mice specifically in principal cells of the collecting duct (strain C57BL/6 N, RRID: MGI:2159965), Nfat5fl/fl mice were crossed with Aqp2-Cre+/− mice, which express Cre recombinase under the control of the Aqp2 promoter. The integration of the Cre transgene disrupts one allele of Aqp2; therefore, only Aqp2-Cre+/−Nfat5fl/fl mice and Aqp2-Cre+/− littermate controls were analyzed. For distal tubule and collecting duct-specific Nfat5 deficiency (KspCre+/−Nfat5fl/fl), Nfat5fl/fl animals were bred with KspCre+/− (Ksp1.3-Cre) mice expressing Cre under the control of a 1329 bp Ksp-cadherin (CdH16) promoter fragment (Ksp1.3Cre mice obtained from The Jackson Laboratory). Male and female mice were involved in this study. Sex was not considered as a biological variable.

sec.title: Cell culture and cell transfection
sec.p: For in vitro experiments mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEF; ATCC-No.: #SCRC-1008, RRID: CVCL_9115) were used. This cell line shows robust BPGM expression and provides acceptable comparability to renal BPGM regulated observations [14]. Cells were cultured at 21% O2, 5% CO2, and 37 °C in RPMI-1640 medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum, 1% penicillin-streptomycin, and 1% L-glutamine. Cells were passaged at ~ 80% confluence using PBS washes and trypsin-EDTA. Experiments were conducted using cells between passages 3 and 18.

Gene knockdown was achieved by transfecting cells with target-specific small interfering RNAs (siRNAs). SMARTpool siRNAs (comprising four distinct siRNAs per target gene (Supplementary Table S1); ON-TARGETplus Mouse Nfat5 siRNA: #L-058868-01-0020; ON-TARGETplus Mouse Bpgm siRNA: #L-058581-01-0005; ON-TARGETplus Non-targeting Pool: #D-001810-10-20) were used at a final concentration of 25 nM. Transfections were performed using DharmaFECT 1 reagent according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Briefly, siRNA and transfection reagent were diluted in serum-free medium, incubated separately for 5 min at room temperature, then combined and incubated for another 20 min before being added to the cells. Transfection using mock siRNA served as control. Knockdown efficiency was confirmed at the mRNA level by quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR) and at the protein level by Western blotting.

To induce hyperosmotic stress, 0.1 M NaCl, 0.2 M mannose, or 0.2 M sucrose was added to the culture medium 24 h post-transfection as indicated, raising the osmolality to approximately 450 mOsmol/kg. Control medium had an osmolality of 270 ± 10 mOsmol/kg. Osmolality was verified using a freezing point osmometer.

sec.title: Cell counting
sec.p: Cell numbers were determined using the TC20™ Automated Cell Counter (Bio-Rad Laboratories GmbH, Germany) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Trypan blue exclusion was used to assess cell viability.

sec.title: Glucose/ lactate measurements
sec.p: Cell culture supernatants were collected after experiments and centrifuged at 1,000 rpm for 1 min at room temperature to remove cellular debris. Glucose and lactate concentrations were measured with an ABL800 Flex PLUS blood gas analyzer.

sec.title: qPCR
sec.p: Quantitative PCR (qPCR) was carried out as previously outlined [25]. Specifically, for in vivo experiments, tissue samples were snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen and subsequently pulverized before RNA extraction. For in vitro experiments, cultured cells were washed three times with ice-cold PBS and then lysed directly in QIAzol Lysis reagent (Cat. #79306, Qiagen), according to the manufacturer’s protocol. RNA concentration and purity were assessed using the NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc.). Complementary DNA (cDNA) synthesis was carried out with random primers and Superscript II reverse transcriptase (Cat. #18064071, Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc.). qPCR was performed on a CFX Connect system (Bio-Rad Laboratories, Inc.) using SYBR Green Master Mix (Cat. #4367659, Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc.). Specific primers were designed using Primer-BLAST (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/tools/primer-blast/index) and synthesized by TIB Molbiol Syntheselabor GmbH, with all sequences detailed in Supplementary Table S2. The qPCR cycling protocol included a 10-minute initial denaturation at 95 °C, followed by 40 cycles of 20 s at 95 °C and 40 s at 60 °C. All measurements were conducted in technical triplicates. The mean values of triplicates were normalized to the housekeeping gene β-actin using the ΔΔCt method [26].

sec.title: Western blotting
sec.p: Western blotting was conducted following previously described protocols [25]. In detail, cells were lysed in buffer containing 50 mM Tris (pH 6.8), 4 M urea, 1% sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), and 12.5 mM dithiothreitol. Protein concentrations were measured using a NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc.). Equal amounts of protein were separated by SDS–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis and transferred onto nitrocellulose membranes. After blocking for 1 h at room temperature in 5% skimmed milk in TBS-T, membranes were incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies (Supplementary Table S3). HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies (Supplementary Table S3) were applied for 1 h at room temperature. Detection was performed with WesternBright chemiluminescent substrate (Cat. #541014, Biozym Scientific GmbH) and imaged using a Chemostar Imager (Intas Science Imaging Instruments GmbH). Band intensities were quantified using Image Studio Lite software (LI-COR Biosciences), and protein expression levels were normalized to tubulin (TUBB2B).

sec.title: Immunofluorescence staining
sec.p: Immunofluorescence was performed on both paraffin-embedded tissue sections and cultured MEF cells. For tissue, samples were dehydrated, embedded in paraffin, and cut into 1.5 μm sections. After rehydration, antigen retrieval was carried out by pressure-cooking for 12 min in 1 x Target Retrieval Solution (Cat. #S1699, Agilent Technologies). Sections were blocked for 1 h at room temperature in 5% skimmed milk in TBS-T, followed by overnight incubation with primary antibodies (Supplementary Table S3) diluted in Antibody Diluent (Cat. #S3022, Agilent). After three washes in TBS-T, appropriate secondary antibodies (Supplementary Table S3) were applied for 1 h at room temperature. Slides were mounted in 60% glycerol/1× PBS containing 584 mM sucrose. For antibody stripping, sections were washed in TBS-T and subjected to antigen retrieval as described above before re-staining. For MEF cell immunofluorescence, cells grown on coverslips were treated for 24 h under hyperosmotic conditions, washed with PBS, and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 10 min. After three PBS washes, cells were permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100 for 30 min and blocked in 5% skimmed milk for 1 h at room temperature. Cells were incubated overnight at 4 °C with a primary antibody (Supplementary Table S3) diluted in Antibody Diluent, followed by 3 washes with PBS. Afterwards, cells were incubation with an appropriate secondary antibody and Hoechst 33,342 (Cat. #62249, Thermo Scientific™) for 1 h at room temperature. Coverslips were washed and mounted using Immu-Mount™ (Cat. #9990402, Epredia Netherlands B.V.). Slides and coverslips were imaged using an Eclipse Ti2-A microscope equipped with a DS-Qi2 camera (Nikon). Multichannel images were aligned and overlaid using BigStitcher in FIJI/ImageJ. After registration via Load & Stitch Multiple XMLs, fused overlays were exported as TIFFs.

sec.title: Next-generation sequencing (NGS)
sec.p: RNA for transcriptome analysis was extracted as described. Bulk RNA sequencing was carried out by QIAGEN Genomic Services (https://www.qiagen.com/us/applications/next-generation-sequencing/genomic-services/rna-sequencing-services/mrna-ngs-seq-service). Library was prepared with the QIAseq UPX 3’ Transcriptome Kit (QIAGEN) using 2.5 µl purified RNA. Unique molecular indexes (UMI) were attached during reverse transcription into cDNA and the quality of libraries was checked by capillary electrophoresis (Agilent DNA 7500 Chip, Agilent Technologies, Inc., USA). After quantification via qPCR, libraries were equimolarly pooled. A NextSeq 500 instrument (Illumina, Inc., USA) was used for sequencing following manufactures instructions (100 bp read length for read 1, 27 bp for read 2). After demultiplexing raw data using the bcl2fastq2 software (Illumina, Inc., USA), FASTQ files were generated for each sample. Further processing of the FASTQ files was carried out with the “Demultiplex QIAseq UPX 3’ reads” tool from the CLC Genomics Workbench 21.0.4. The “Quantify QIAseq UPX 3’ workflow” (default settings) was used to annotate reads with UMIs, trimming poly(A) and adapters, and deduplication based on UMIs followed by mapping the reads to the Mouse genome GRCm38 v. 80 together with the ENSEMBL GRCm38 v. 86 gene annotation. The “Empirical analysis of DGE” algorithm was used for differential gene expression analysis with the “Exact Test” for two-group comparisons by Robinson and Smyth from the EdgeR Bioconductor package [27]. Genes with less than 10 counts summed across all samples were excluded from the analysis. Normalization was performed by variance stabilizing transformation from the DESeq2 R package (version 1.28.1) [28].

sec.title: Gene set overrepresentation analysis (ORA)
sec.p: To check for overrepresented pathways ORA was performed using the clusterProfiler package [29] for R. The annotation table “Biological processe” [30, 31] was used for ORA. The obtained pathway list was simplified with the simplify function from the GOSemSim R package [32]. Detailed settings for ORA analysis are summarized in Supplementary Table S4. Data were visualized with the enrichplot R package [33].

sec.title: Correlation analysis
sec.p: Correlation of NFAT5 and BPGM transcript levels were performed as described in Mrowka et al. [34]. Briefly, human transcriptomic datasets were sourced from the Stanford Microarray Database [35], as utilized in the study by Stuart et al. [36]. This resource comprises experiments from a wide range of independent studies, including gene expression profiles from cancer tissues, cell lines, and various human tissues, as well as data related to biological processes such as the cell cycle, cellular stress, signaling pathways, and apoptosis. Details regarding data preprocessing and normalization procedures can be found in Stuart et al. [36]. Experiments lacking expression data for either gene were excluded from correlation analyses.

sec.title: Genome wide CpG analysis of human and mouse promotor regions
sec.p: Promoter sequences containing 2000 bp for all human or mouse genes were obtained from https://www.ensembl.org/biomart in March 2025. For the human genome assembly GRCh38.p14 and for the mouse genome assembly GRCm38 were used. The values for the number of CpG Islands and GC content were calculated using custom python code. The following criteria were applied for the definition of a CpG island: (1) a minimum length of 200 bp, (2) a GC content of at least 50%, and (3) an observed-to-expected CpG ratio of at least 0.6. The dataset was analyzed on a genome wide scale.

sec.title: Statistics
sec.p: Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism (version 9, USA). Outliers were identified using the ROUT method with a Q value of 5% [37]. For in vitro experiments using cell lines, a normal distribution was assumed. Comparisons involving more than two groups were analyzed using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post hoc test. For in vivo tissue samples, normality was assessed using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. For normally distributed datasets with more than two groups, variance equality was evaluated, and if this assumption was violated (defined as a more than two-fold difference in standard deviations), a Brown–Forsythe ANOVA followed by Dunnett’s T3 post hoc test was applied. For non-normally distributed datasets involving more than two groups, the Kruskal–Wallis test followed by Dunn’s post hoc test was used. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

sec.title: BPGM expression is induced by osmotic stress and associated with NFAT5 activity
sec.p: While BPGM is well characterized in erythrocytes for its role in 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate production and oxygen release, its function in non-erythroid cells remains largely unknown. One strategy to uncover novel intracellular roles is to study conditions under which gene expression is dynamically regulated, based on the idea that functional relevance is often linked to gene expression control. In a recent study, we identified osmotic stress as a strong regulator of BPGM expression [14], prompting us to explore its role in cellular osmoadaptation.

To test stimulus specificity, we exposed cells to NaCl (100 mM), mannose (200 mM), and sucrose (200 mM), each raising osmolality to ~ 450 mOsmol/kg. After 6 h, all three conditions induced Bpgm mRNA upregulation (Fig. 1a). At 24 h, expression remained high with sucrose, while responses to NaCl and mannose declined (Fig. 1b). This likely reflects differential adaptation kinetics: NaCl promotes rapid ionic responses, mannose induces intermediate adaptation, and sucrose, being poorly permeable, maintains extracellular hyperosmolarity longer. Despite these transcript-level differences, BPGM protein levels were elevated under all conditions at 24 h, indicating a sustained response (Fig. 1c).

Since BPGM is regulated at both mRNA and protein levels, transcriptional or post-transcriptional mechanisms, affecting mRNA stability, are likely involved. To identify potential regulators, we analyzed human transcriptomic databases [35, 36] and performed a correlation analysis across 509 distinct experimental conditions, which revealed a strong positive correlation of BPGM with NFAT5, a critical transcription factor involved in osmotic stress responses (Fig. 1d).

Support for NFAT5-mediated regulation came from Nfat5 knockout models [13], where Bpgm mRNA was reduced in both Ksp-Cre and Aqp2-Cre driven deletions. While Ksp-Cre targets distal tubules broadly, Aqp2-Cre is restricted to principal cells of the collecting duct. Accordingly, Bpgm was downregulated in cortex and medulla in Ksp-Cre, but only in the cortex in Aqp2-Cre mice, indicating segment-specific NFAT5 regulation (Fig. 1e). To validate NFAT5 inactivation, we analyzed Akr1b1, encoding Aldose Reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of the polyol pathway and a known NFAT5 target. Akr1b1 was strongly downregulated in both models, confirming effective loss of NFAT5 activity and supporting the specificity of Bpgm regulation (Fig. 1f).

sec.title: Segment-specific expression of BPGM and NFAT5 in the distal nephron
sec.p: To assess whether NFAT5 could directly regulate BPGM, we examined their spatial co-expression in mouse kidney sections using immunofluorescence with established segment markers: calbindin (distal convoluted tubule and connecting tubule) and aquaporin-2 (collecting duct). Both, BPGM and NFAT5 showed strong co-localization with calbindin and AQP2, indicating expression in overlapping cell types of the distal nephron (Fig. 2a, b).

MEF cells proved suitable for in vitro studies, as proteomic profiling revealed strong overlap between Bpgm-deficient MEFs and Bpgm-knockout mouse kidneys [14]. Moreover, MEFs express NFAT5 and show nuclear translocation upon osmotic stress, supporting their use as a model to study BPGM regulation by NFAT5 (Fig. 2c).

(b) Magnified view of cortical DCT region showing NFAT5 in calbindin-positive cells. (c) Immunofluorescence of NFAT5 in mouse embryonic fibroblast (MEF) cells showing nuclear translocation upon sucrose-induced osmotic stress (200 mM, 6 h). Scale bars: 50 μm

sec.title: NFAT5 knockdown attenuates BPGM induction under hyperosmotic stress
sec.p: To test whether Bpgm expression under hyperosmotic conditions is functionally dependent on NFAT5, we performed siRNA-mediated knockdown in MEF cells and exposed them to control or osmotic stress conditions (200 mM sucrose, 24 h). Western blot analysis (Fig. 3a) revealed strong induction of NFAT5 protein under osmotic stress, which was effectively suppressed by si-Nfat5 mediated knockdown (Fig. 3a, b). BPGM protein was also markedly increased in response to stress and significantly reduced by Nfat5 knockdown (Fig. 3c). These findings were corroborated at the transcript level: qPCR showed robust Nfat5 and Bpgm mRNA upregulation under hypertonic stress, both of which were significantly diminished by Nfat5 knockdown (Fig. 3d and e). Notably, at the mRNA level, Bpgm expression was not fully abolished by Nfat5 knockdown, suggesting a partial but significant dependency on NFAT5. This may reflect residual NFAT5 activity, possibly due to incomplete silencing and continued nuclear translocation of remaining protein under stress conditions. Supporting this notion, Akr1b1 expression, used as a positive NFAT5 target, was also strongly reduced but not restored to baseline level (Fig. 3f).

(a) Representative Western blot of NFAT5 and BPGM under control and hyperosmotic conditions (200 mM sucrose, 24 h), with siRNA-mediated knockdown (si-Nfat5) or control (si-mock). (b–c) Quantification of NFAT5 (b) and BPGM (c) protein levels. (d–e) mRNA levels of Nfat5 (d) and Bpgm (e) assessed by qPCR. (f) Akr1b1 expression serves as a control for NFAT5 activity. (b-f) Box plots show the median with lower and upper quartile as box. Whiskers show the minimum and maximum range of the values. Statistical analysis was performed using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post hoc test. p-values are shown in the figure

sec.p: Together, our findings support a model in which NFAT5 may contribute to the regulation of BPGM in distal nephron segments, based on functional in vitro data and co-expression in vivo.

sec.title: Context-specific role of BPGM in osmoadaptive gene regulation
sec.p: To further explore downstream effects of BPGM, we performed transcriptomic profiling (RNA-seq) following Bpgm knockdown under control and hyperosmotic conditions (200 mM sucrose, 24 h). For Bpgm knockdown verification see Supplementary Figure S1. Under basal conditions, 40 genes were differentially expressed, whereas under hyperosmotic stress, 110 genes were regulated (adjusted p < 0.05). Strikingly, only 5 genes overlapped between both conditions (Fig. 4a), suggesting that BPGM modulates distinct transcriptional networks depending on the osmotic state. Since NFAT5 is active under hyperosmotic conditions and drives BPGM expression, these data support the concept of a stress-induced NFAT5–BPGM axis, where BPGM contributes to context-specific gene regulation.

To validate and illustrate this context dependency, we chose five representative genes that were selectively affected by Bpgm knockdown under hyperosmotic stress, but not under control conditions (Figs. 4b–f): Ctnnb1 (β-catenin 1), a key component of Wnt signaling and cell–cell adhesion; Wsb1 (WD repeat and SOCS box-containing 1), an E3 ubiquitin ligase involved in hypoxia signaling and protein degradation; Fscn1, encoding the actin-bundling protein fascin-1, important for cytoskeletal dynamics; Daglb (diacylglycerol lipase beta), implicated in lipid signaling; and Actr6 (actin related protein 6), a component of the INO80 chromatin remodeling complex. Interestingly, no reports were found linking these genes individually to NFAT5-mediated osmotic responses. Especially Wsb1 and Fscn1 that show no elevation by hypertonic conditions per se, indicate that BPGM specifically modulates the hyperosmotic cellular response.

Thus, our findings suggest that BPGM acts downstream of NFAT5 to influence osmotic stress-responsive gene networks and identify novel candidate genes that may belong to previously unrecognized branches of the NFAT5-BPGM-mediated osmoadaptive network. Based on this distinct transcriptional signature, we focused all further investigations on the osmotic stress condition to better understand the functional relevance of BPGM in this context.

sec.title: NFAT5 and BPGM regulate overlapping transcriptional programs under osmotic stress
sec.p: To further investigate the relationship between NFAT5 and BPGM, we compared transcriptomic changes induced by knockdown of either gene under identical hyperosmotic stress conditions (200 mM sucrose, 24 h). Knockdown of Nfat5 resulted in 2,616 significantly regulated genes, consistent with its established role as a master regulator of osmoadaptation (Fig. 5a). Notably, Nfat5 knockdown also led to downregulation of BPGM (see Fig. 3), suggesting that some of the observed transcriptomic changes may reflect secondary effects due to reduced BPGM expression. To determine whether BPGM alone could account for a subset of these effects, we next analyzed Bpgm knockdown under the same conditions. This revealed 110 differentially expressed genes, 61 of which overlapped with those regulated by Nfat5 knockdown (Fig. 5a), suggesting that over half of the BPGM-dependent transcriptomic response may be embedded within the broader NFAT5 regulatory network.

Strikingly, functional enrichment analyses revealed that both knockdowns impacted similar gene ontologies, including cell cycle regulation, TGF (transforming growth factor)-β signaling, response to hypoxia, and methylation (Figs. 5b–d). These findings suggest that despite the difference in scale, BPGM and NFAT5 modulate overlapping biological pathways under hyperosmotic conditions.

sec.p: The striking overlap in functional pathways, despite a 20-fold difference in gene numbers, suggests that BPGM may act as a precision modulator within the broader NFAT5 response. To unravel this potential role, we next interrogated the shared signatures between both knockdowns, focusing on key regulatory modules within the osmoadaptive landscape.

sec.title: Validation of the NFAT5–BPGM axis in regulating hypoxia-associated genes under hyperosmotic stress
sec.p: Prompted by the enrichment of “response to hypoxia” pathways in both Nfat5 and Bpgm knockdown datasets, we next aimed to examine this aspect more closely. A schematic overview (Fig. 6a) summarizes the experimental setup and the proposed regulation of NFAT5 and BPGM across all conditions. Under hyperosmotic stress, hypoxia inducible factor-1α (Hif1a) mRNA was strongly induced (Fig. 6b). This induction was abolished by Nfat5 knockdown and moderately but significantly attenuated by Bpgm knockdown.

Likewise, established HIF-1 target genes (Hk2: hexokinase-2; Phd3 alias Egln3: egl-9 family hypoxia inducible factor 3, and AldoC: aldolase C) exhibited a similar expression pattern (Figs. 6c–e), with robust induction under stress conditions, complete suppression in the si-Nfat5 group, and partial reduction in the si-Bpgm group. In contrast, heme oxygenase-1 (Hmox-1), a stress-responsive gene regulated by multiple pathways including oxidative stress, inflammation, and hypoxia, was induced by osmotic stress but not significantly affected by either knockdown (Fig. 6f). These findings indicate that the NFAT5–BPGM axis contributes to hypoxia-relevant transcriptional responses, highlighting an underappreciated link between hyperosmotic and hypoxic adaptation mechanisms.

(a) Schematic overview illustrating experimental conditions and proposed expression changes of NFAT5 and BPGM under hyperosmotic stress (200 mM sucrose, 24 h) in control (si-mock), and Nfat5 and Bpgm knockdown (si-Nfat5 and si-Bpgm, respectively) conditions. (b–f) Quantitative PCR analysis of mRNA expression for hypoxia-related genes under normo-osmotic control (si-mock), hyperosmotic stress (si-mock), and hyperosmotic knockdown conditions (si-Nfat5, si-Bpgm). Gene expression was normalized to β-actin. Box plots show the median with lower and upper quartile as box. Whiskers show the minimum and maximum range of the values. Statistical analysis was performed using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post hoc test. p-values are indicated in the figure

sec.title: BPGM and NFAT5 modulate cell proliferation and glycolytic adaptation during osmotic stress
sec.p: Our data further implicated “cell cycle” pathways in both Nfat5- and Bpgm-deficient cells. To validate this, we quantified total live cell numbers under control and hyperosmotic conditions (Fig. 7a). Osmotic stress reduced cell numbers significantly, and this effect was further exacerbated by either Nfat5 or Bpgm knockdown, suggesting that both NFAT5 activation and BPGM expression contribute to the maintenance of cell numbers under stress conditions. This is consistent with a recent report showing that Bpgm knockdown accelerates apoptosis under hypertonic stress [14]. Moreover, Ki-67 mRNA, a marker of proliferation, was significantly reduced under hyperosmotic conditions and further suppressed by knockdown of either Nfat5 or Bpgm (Fig. 7b).

To assess the relevance of these findings to humans, we analyzed BPGM-correlated genes in human transcriptomic datasets, as indicated in Fig. 1d, and found significant enrichment of ontologies associated with chromosome organization, DNA replication, and cell cycle processes (Fig. 7c), affirming that the link between BPGM and proliferative control is also relevant in humans.

While “glycolysis” did not emerge directly as a regulated pathway in the NGS analyses, BPGM is known to modulate glycolytic flux [14]. To explore this connection, we quantified glucose consumption and lactate production under osmotic stress (Figs. 7d–e). Both were significantly increased in response to hyperosmolarity, consistent with an enhanced glycolytic rate. Notably, knockdown of either Nfat5 or Bpgm further amplified these effects. These findings suggest that NFAT5 and BPGM limit the extent of glycolytic activation under osmotic stress, potentially to fine-tune energy metabolism, prevent metabolic overcompensation, or avoid excessive production of osmolytes such as lactate. This highlights a previously unrecognized function of the NFAT5–BPGM axis in balancing glycolysis and stress response.

sec.title: Genes co-regulated by NFAT5 and BPGM are enriched for CpG-rich promoter regions
sec.p: Increased glycolytic activity is known to influence chromatin modifications, as glycolytic intermediates such as 3-phosphoglycerate, pyruvate, and acetyl-CoA can affect DNA and histone methylation [38–40]. Given BPGM’s known function as a glycolytic modulator and its inhibitory effect on glycolytic flux [14], we hypothesized that BPGM might link metabolic adaptation to epigenetic regulation.

To test this, we analyzed the promoter architecture of genes that were co-regulated by NFAT5 and BPGM under osmotic stress (n = 61; see Fig. 5a). Using publicly available promoter sequence data, we examined CpG island frequency in the − 2000 to − 1 bp region upstream of the transcription start site. In human sequences, these genes exhibited a markedly higher number of CpG islands compared to a background gene set (Fig. 8a), which was confirmed in mouse promoter sequences (Fig. 8b) and thus indicates evolutionary conservation. Furthermore, observed/expected CpG ratios were significantly elevated in both human (Fig. 8c) and mouse (Fig. 8d) genes of interest, supporting the hypothesis that these genes are embedded in CpG-rich regulatory regions.

Further analyses of GC content using the same set of 61 genes, confirmed that the NFAT5/ BPGM co-regulated genes display a significantly higher GC content in their promoter regions compared to background genes (Supplementary Figure S2a, b).

Together, these analyses indicate that promoters of genes co-regulated by NFAT5 and BPGM are significantly enriched in CpG islands and exhibit elevated GC content. In line with the marked differential expression of genes associated with the GO-term “methylation” (see Fig. 5c and d), our data suggest that epigenetic mechanisms may contribute to their regulation under hyperosmotic conditions.

sec.title: Fibrosis develops in vivo following loss of either NFAT5 or BPGM
sec.p: Our transcriptomic in vitro analyses revealed a significant enrichment of TGFβ-related signaling pathways in both Bpgm- and Nfat5-knockdown conditions (Fig. 5b–d). This finding was confirmed by the upregulation of two key factors, collagen type I alpha 1 (Col1a1) and transforming growth factor beta 1 (Tgfb1), in the same knockdown conditions compared to controls (Fig. 9a, b). Since these pathways are tightly linked to fibrosis but challenging to capture in short-term cell culture, we examined them in distal tubule-specific Bpgm- and Nfat5-KO mice. Here, the knockout persists for 5–21 days, allowing more pronounced fibrotic changes to develop. qPCR analysis confirmed upregulation of Col1a1 and Tgfb1 in mouse kidneys as a result of tubular Nfat5 or Bpgm knockout (Fig. 9c, d).

sec.p: Immunohistochemical staining in kidneys of both KspCre-driven knockout models confirmed increased COL1A1 deposition in distal and connecting tubules as a hallmark of fibrotic remodeling (Fig. 10). Together, these in vivo results provide a consistent picture across experimental approaches and support the conclusion that loss of BPGM or NFAT5 promotes pro-fibrotic signaling in the kidney.

sec.p: Together, these findings demonstrate that pro-fibrotic transcriptional signatures observed in vitro upon loss of NFAT5 or BPGM translate into structural fibrotic changes in vivo. This underscores the physiological relevance of the NFAT5-BPGM axis in maintaining tubular homeostasis.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this study, we hypothesized that BPGM acts as a key metabolic effector in hypertonic environments. Our results indicate that loss of BPGM disrupts adaptive gene expression, exacerbates cell stress, and alters hypoxic signaling under hyperosmotic conditions. We show that BPGM expression is regulated by the tonicity-responsive transcription factor NFAT5, placing BPGM as a novel downstream effector in NFAT5-mediated osmoregulation. Notably, BPGM influences a broad range of genes overlapping with NFAT5-dependent transcriptional programs. We suggest that modulation of glycolytic flux via BPGM contributes to adaptive gene expression in hypertonic stress, potentially linking metabolic regulation to epigenetic plasticity. This points toward a previously unrecognized metabolic-epigenetic axis in osmoadaptation.

Clinically, distal nephron cells, particularly those in cortical tubular segments where BPGM is constitutively and inducibly expressed [14], may experience hyperosmolar stress under various (patho-)physiological and therapeutic conditions. While high osmolarity in the renal medulla is well described, cortical osmolarity is generally lower but can still be significantly elevated locally. For example, local hypoxia promotes a shift toward anaerobic metabolism, elevating intracellular lactate and thereby enhancing osmotic stress. Dehydration may further amplify osmolality in the late distal tubule and connecting tubule through antidiuretic hormone (ADH)-dependent water reabsorption. In diabetes mellitus, glucosuria and ketoacidosis increase tubular osmotic load, particularly under SGLT2 (solute carrier family 5 member 2, SLC5A2) inhibition [41–44]. Additionally, any filtered but non-reabsorbed osmolyte, such as iodinated contrast media or ethylene glycol [45–47] transiently raises tubular osmolality and can injure epithelial cells. Common diuretics also alter tubular osmotic conditions by modifying solute delivery or ion transport in distal segments. These clinical and pharmacological conditions represent settings in which our findings may be particularly relevant.

Osmotic stress induces cell cycle arrest in renal epithelial cells [48–50], shifting resources towards stress adaptation and repair. In our study, knockdown of either Nfat5 or Bpgm amplifies cell cycle arrest under hypertonic stress, suggesting a role for both factors in protecting cells from excessive stress-induced growth arrest. While involvement of NFAT5 is well-documented, our transcriptomic data suggest that BPGM participates in the regulation of cell cycle progression, as corresponding genes are modulated by NFAT5 driven hyperosmotic adaptation, but are similarly influenced by Nfat5 and Bpgm knockdown. This points toward a NFAT5-BPGM cascade, with cell cycle arrest being, at least partially, downstream of BPGM.

Interestingly, BPGM, as a glycolytic enzyme, is not expected to regulate gene expression directly. Nevertheless, our data reveal that genes similarly affected by either Nfat5 or Bpgm knockdown under hypertonic conditions are enriched for DNA methylation–related regulatory features, suggesting an indirect link between BPGM activity and transcriptional control. These inferences are based on converging lines of evidence, including transcriptional signatures, pathway enrichment analyses, and promoter architecture. Specifically, genes co-regulated under hyperosmotic stress by either Nfat5 or Bpgm knockdown were significantly enriched for CpG-rich promoter regions and associated with methylation-related gene ontologies.

A plausible mechanistic connection between altered BPGM expression and modulation of the NFAT5-dependent transcriptional response emerges from changes in cellular glucose metabolism. We show that knockdown of Nfat5 as well as Bpgm results in accelerated glycolysis, as evidenced by increased glucose consumption and lactate production. These findings indicate that NFAT5-dependent induction of BPGM is required to appropriately regulate glycolytic flux and, thus, glucose metabolism under hypertonic stress.

BPGM, through its enzymatic product 2,3-BPG, is known to inhibit glycolysis [14, 17, 51]. Moreover, previous studies have shown that BPGM modulates levels of glycolytic intermediates [52], which are increasingly recognized as regulators of gene expression via epigenetic mechanisms [38–40]. For instance, according to the Warburg effect, cells (most prominently cancer cells) favor glycolysis over oxidative phosphorylation, leading to accumulation of glycolytic and tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle intermediates that directly or indirectly impact epigenetic modifications [53]. Consequently, the accelerated glycolysis observed in Bpgm-deficient cells may disrupt the balance of key metabolites such as acetyl-CoA and S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), essential cofactors for histone and DNA modifications [54]. Perturbations in TCA cycle homeostasis may also influence levels of 2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG), an oncometabolite that regulates α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases involved in DNA and histone demethylation [55].

Together, our findings support a model in which the magnitude and composition of the NFAT5-driven transcriptional response under hypertonic stress is not solely determined by NFAT5 activation itself, but is critically shaped by BPGM-dependent metabolic adaptation. By modulating glycolytic flux and the availability of metabolic intermediates, BPGM appears to influence the chromatin environment in which NFAT5 operates, thereby fine-tuning NFAT5-driven gene expression.

Beyond effects on cell cycle regulation, a prominent functional readout of this NFAT5-BPGM-dependent transcriptional program is the HIF-1 response. HIF-1α, a key transcription factor in hypoxia, is partly regulated by promoter methylation [56]. NFAT5 and HIF-1α have previously been described as parallel or context-dependent stress response pathways, with reports indicating either independent activation or mutual restriction depending on cell type and stimulus [57–60]. In our study, hyperosmotic stress induced both expression and activation of HIF-1α, as reflected by increased levels of canonical HIF-1 target genes. Notably, knockdown of either Nfat5 or Bpgm resulted in a marked reduction of Hif1a abundance and target gene expression, indicating that an intact NFAT5-BPGM axis is required for full activation of the HIF-1 response under hyperosmotic stress. Importantly, our findings do not imply that osmotic stress directly causes hypoxia; rather, they suggest that NFAT5-dependent transcriptional and BPGM-mediated metabolic adjustment enables an appropriate HIF-1 response under hypertonic conditions. However, the precise molecular mechanisms linking NFAT5-BPGM-dependent metabolic changes to HIF-1α regulation remain to be defined and targeted analyses of DNA methylation, histone modifications, and chromatin accessibility will be essential to delineate how metabolic cues are translated into stable or reversible epigenetic states during osmoadaptation. Importantly, our findings are consistent with previous proteomic data showing that tubular, inducible Bpgm knockout in the mouse kidney inhibits the “hypoxia” and “oxidative phosphorylation” pathways [14].

Beyond the kidney, BPGM is expressed in other metabolically active or stress-exposed tissues, including placenta and tumor cells [16, 61], which are characterized by dynamic metabolic and epigenetic remodeling. While the functional relevance of an NFAT5-BPGM axis in these contexts remains to be established, our findings raise the possibility that similar metabolic-transcriptional coupling mechanisms may operate in non-renal settings, particularly where hypoxic and metabolic stress responses overlap. Thus, our results support the broader concept that transcriptional stress responses can be modulated by changes in glucose metabolism, a principle that may extend to other systems exposed to combined metabolic and osmotic or hypoxic stress.

In summary, the transcriptional overlap between NFAT5 and BPGM targets under hyperosmotic stress, and the observation that Bpgm knockdown limits the full induction of NFAT5-responsive genes, point toward a hierarchical but interdependent relationship. While NFAT5 transcriptionally induces Bpgm, the presence of BPGM appears to support or even potentiate the NFAT5-driven transcriptional program, likely through metabolic-epigenetic coupling. In this light, BPGM emerges as a mediator of NFAT5 function, acting downstream while feeding back on transcriptional output by shaping the chromatin environment. Disruption of the NFAT5-BPGM axis compromises osmoprotective gene expression, consistent with renal fibrosis observed in mice lacking either NFAT5 or BPGM [13, 14].
